content: Pediatric Basic Life Support (BLS) is a critical life-saving intervention that includes the administration of high-quality cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) and rescue breaths, often in conjunction with the use of an Automated External Defibrillator (AED). Bystander CPR, performed by individuals present at the scene of a cardiac arrest, plays a pivotal role in improving survival rates for children experiencing out-of-hospital cardiac arrest. Research conducted by Maryam Y. Naim and colleagues has demonstrated that communities where bystander CPR is more commonly practiced exhibit significantly better survival outcomes in children under the age of 18 who suffer from out-of-hospital cardiac arrest. Two separate studies, encompassing a total of 781 children, revealed that approximately 50% of cardio-respiratory arrests in children under the age of 12 months occur outside of a hospital setting. Several factors are associated with a favorable prognosis upon the child’s arrival at the emergency department. These include: A short interval between the cardiac arrest event and the child’s arrival at the hospital. A duration of resuscitation efforts in the emergency department that is less than 20 minutes. The administration of fewer than two doses of epinephrine during resuscitation efforts.
